newsitem.title: ITALY: New Italian trial ordered for ex-SS man Priebke.
newsitem.headline: New Italian trial ordered for ex-SS man Priebke.

text.p: Italy's highest appeal court ordered a re-trial of war crimes suspect and former SS captain Erich Priebke on Tuesday for his involvement in the 1944 Nazi massacre of 335 men and boys.

The Court of Cassation annulled a controversial August 1 verdict at Priebke's first trial which found him guilty of multiple murder but ordered him freed because of mitigating circumstances and a statute of limitations.
"It is a marvellous day, but also a sad one," said Rosetta Stame, one of a group of relatives of victims of the massacre who broke into applause at the court on hearing the ruling.
"On one hand, we've won. But no-one can imagine that what we've gone through in these past months is over yet," said Stame. Her father, an opera singer, was killed in the massacre.
Velio di Rezzo, the 83-year-old German's lawyer, said the ruling was "absolutely unjust".
He said he would discuss it with Priebke on Wednesday at the Rome jail where he has been held on remand since the verdict pending the outcome of appeals and a German extradition request.
The Court of Cassation ruled in favour of a motion by the prosecution and civil plaintiffs representing victims' families.

It granted their request to overturn a lower appeal court's decision in July rejecting their bid to dismiss the presiding judge at Priebke's military court trial, Agostino Quistelli, on grounds of alleged bias in favour of the accused.

"This is the redemption of the Italian justice system," said Shimon Samuels, director of international affairs for the Los Angeles-based Simon Wiesenthal Center, which tracks former Nazis and which closely followed the Priebke case.
Military prosecutor Antonino Intelisano told Reuters that a new trial would be held before a military court with different judges. "It is a decision which speaks for itself," he said.
Priebke went on trial on May 8 accused of complicity in multiple homicide over the killing of 335 men and boys at the Ardeatine Caves south of Rome in March 1944.
The trial ended in a 2-1 verdict by the three judges that while Priebke had taken part in the massacre, the worst atrocity committed in Italy in World War Two, he could not be jailed.

Priebke, who had lived openly for almost 50 years in Argentina, was blocked inside the courthouse by angry protesters and re-arrested hours later when Germany said it intended to extradite him for a war crimes trial there.
Di Rezze said he planned to seek Priebke's release into house arrest. He has been held in jail in Italy since his extradition from Argentina last November 21.

Samuels said Intelisano told him he might seek to re-try Priebke together with former SS major Karl Hass, who admitted involvement in the Ardeatine Caves massacre when he testified as a prosecution witness at the first trial.
Hass, 84, is being held under house arrest at a private clinic near Rome. He broke his pelvis in a fall from a hotel balcony in June while trying to flee and avoid giving testimony.

Samuels said Intelisano indicated the trial could be held within three to four months. "We would like it to be prompt because of the age of the two and we hope there will be no bureaucratic entanglements to delay swift justice."
The Ardeatine Caves massacre took place in reprisal for a partisan bomb attack on German soldiers in Rome. Seventy-five of the victims were Jews.
Priebke admitted shooting two people and checking off names from a list at the caves, but his lawyers argued he should not be held responsible because he had to follow orders.
